stem: The historical mean (expected) return of N annual returns R_1, …, R_N is:
options: the middle return after ranking the N returns from lowest to highest
explanation: The mean adds the returns and divides by N. The compound (geometric) average multiplies growth factors; N − 1 appears only in the sample variance.

stem: Which of the following calls for the POPULATION standard deviation (divide by N)?
options: Estimating one stock's future volatility from its last five annual returns
Judging a fund from ten years of returns in order to forecast its future risk
Measuring the spread of this month's returns across all nine stocks you hold, as the whole group
Using 20 randomly chosen TSX stocks to estimate the volatility of all TSX stocks
explanation: The professor's examples: population = all the stocks in your portfolio; sample = five years of your favourite stock. Whenever the data are only a sample used to estimate something larger, use N − 1.

stem: You have five years of annual returns on your favourite stock and want its standard deviation. Which formula applies?
options: the sample standard deviation, dividing by N − 1
the population standard deviation, dividing by N
the probability-weighted formula Σ p_i (R_i − E[R])²
the geometric average of the five returns
explanation: Five years are only a sample of the stock's possible returns, so use the sample formula. The probability-weighted formula is for forecast states with given probabilities.

stem: How do the population and sample standard deviations of the same set of returns differ?
options: The sample version divides by N and the population version by N − 1, so the population version is larger.
They are always exactly equal once N is greater than 30, so the choice never matters.
The sample version divides by N − 1 instead of N, so it is slightly larger; use it when the data are a sample.
The population version squares the deviations, whereas the sample version uses absolute values instead.
explanation: Same numerator (sum of squared deviations); different divisor. Dividing by the smaller number N − 1 gives the larger σ. The difference shrinks as N grows.

stem: Why does the sample standard deviation divide by N − 1 rather than N?
options: Because the first year of data is always discarded as a start-up observation.
Because dividing by N − 1 makes the answer come out as an exact whole-number percentage.
Because N years of prices give only N − 1 holding periods for which returns are measured.
Because the deviations around the sample's own mean are a little too small; dividing by N − 1 corrects that.
explanation: Deviations measured from the sample's own mean are on average too small, so dividing by N would understate the variance. Using N − 1 adjusts for this.

stem: Which statement about a historical standard deviation is NOT correct?
options: Dividing by N − 1 instead of N gives a smaller standard deviation.
The deviations from the mean always sum to zero.
It is measured in the same units as the returns.
A wider spread of returns around the mean gives a larger value.
explanation: Dividing by N − 1 (the smaller number) makes the variance and standard deviation larger, not smaller.

stem: Over 1926-2016 (U.S. data in the textbook) large-company stocks had an average return of 12.0% and σ = 19.9%; Treasury bills averaged 3.4% with σ = 3.1%. What does this show?
options: Stocks were less risky than T-bills because their average return was higher.
Stocks paid more on average but were far more volatile; T-bill returns stayed close to their average.
Treasury bills were riskier than stocks because their average return was lower.
The two asset classes had the same risk because both averages were positive.
explanation: σ measures how far returns typically fall from their average. 19.9% versus 3.1% shows far greater volatility for stocks, the price of their higher average return.

stem: For any set of historical returns, the deviations (R_i − mean) add up to zero, which gives a quick check on your arithmetic.
options: True
False
explanation: True. Deviations around the mean always cancel to zero (the textbook's 'the sum of the deviations is equal to zero'). If yours do not, the mean is wrong.

stem: Over five years a stock averaged 9.0% per annum. Four of its annual returns were 15%, −6%, 12% and 20%. Find the missing fifth return and then compute the sample standard deviation of the five returns, in % per annum.
solution: Sum of five returns = 5 × 9.0 = 45, so the fifth = 45 − (15 − 6 + 12 + 20) = 45 − 41 = 4%

stem: A population standard deviation of 6.4% per annum was computed from five annual returns (dividing by N). What would the sample standard deviation (dividing by N − 1) of the same five returns be, in % per annum?

steps.label: Sum of squared deviations = N × σ_pop²

errors.label: Scaled the wrong way, by √(4/5)
errors.explain: The sample σ is larger than the population σ, so multiply by √(N/(N − 1)).

errors.label: Multiplied by N/(N − 1) without the square root
errors.explain: N/(N − 1) scales the variance; the standard deviation scales by its square root.

explanation: Both formulas share the sum of squared deviations, so σ_sample = σ_pop × √(N/(N − 1)) = 6.4 × 1.118 = 7.16%.

stem: A stock's returns over the last four years were 8%, 2%, 14% and −4%. Treat the four years as a sample. What is the standard deviation of its returns?
explanation: Mean 5%; squared deviations 9 + 9 + 81 + 81 = 180. Sample: 180/3 = 60, σ = √60 = 7.75%. Dividing by N = 4 gives 6.71% (population formula); 45.00 and 60.00 are variances that were never square-rooted.

stem: The five stocks in Dana's portfolio returned 6%, 10%, 2%, 12% and 5% last month. Treat the five as the whole population. What is the (population) standard deviation of these returns?
explanation: Mean 7%; squared deviations 1 + 9 + 25 + 25 + 4 = 64. Population: 64/5 = 12.8, σ = √12.8 = 3.58%. Dividing by N − 1 = 4 gives 4.00%; 12.80 and 16.00 are unrooted variances.

stem: A normal distribution is completely described by:
options: its mean and its skewness
its mean and its standard deviation
its minimum and maximum
its median and its range
explanation: That is why the normal is so convenient: once you know μ and σ there is nothing else to know. All the probability ranges (68%, 95%, 99%) follow from these two numbers.

stem: For a normal distribution, approximately what share of outcomes lies within two standard deviations of the mean?
options: about 68%
about 99%
about 50%
about 95%
explanation: The rule of thumb is 68% within one σ, 95% within two σ and 99% within three σ.

stem: Which pair of statements about a normal distribution is correct?
options: Within one σ lies about 68%; below the mean minus one σ lies about 32%.
Within one σ lies about 34%; below the mean minus one σ lies about 68%.
Within one σ lies about 68% of outcomes; below the mean minus one σ lies only about 16%.
Within one σ lies about 95%; below the mean minus one σ lies about 5%.
explanation: About 32% lies outside ±1σ, split equally between the two tails, so about 16% lies below μ − σ.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a property of the normal distribution?
options: It is bell-shaped and symmetric around its mean.
It is skewed, with the mean above the median.
It is completely described by its mean and standard deviation.
About 68% of outcomes fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
explanation: The normal is symmetric, so its mean and median coincide; there is no skew.

stem: Why can the normal distribution be used to describe yearly stock returns?
options: Because stock returns are exactly normal in every sample that has been observed.
Because the normal distribution guarantees that no loss ever exceeds three standard deviations.
Because historical returns are roughly mound-shaped and symmetric, and a normal is fully described by μ and σ.
Because the normal distribution removes the need to estimate σ or the mean from data.
explanation: The normal is an approximation, not an exact description: actual distributions are at least roughly mound-shaped and symmetric, which is good enough for the 68/95/99 rules.

stem: U.S. large-company stocks averaged 12.0% with σ = 19.9% over 1926-2016. Treating returns as normal, what does the range −7.9% to 31.9% (12.0% ± 19.9%) tell an investor?
options: About two years in three fall inside this range and about one year in three outside.
The return will fall inside this range in every single year, with no exceptions.
There is about a 95% chance that the annual return falls inside this range.
The return will be below −7.9% in about one year out of three.
explanation: ±1σ covers about 68% (roughly 2/3) of outcomes. About 1/3 of years fall outside, split between above 31.9% and below −7.9% (about 16% each).

stem: A Calgary REIT has annual returns that are roughly normal with a mean of 8.0% and a standard deviation of 12.0%. Using the cumulative normal table, what is the probability of earning more than 20% in a given year, in %?

errors.label: Reported N(1.00), the probability of being below
errors.explain: N(z) is P(R < X). The question asks for the upper tail, so take 1 − N(z).

errors.label: Divided by σ² instead of σ in the z-score
errors.explain: z = (X − μ)/σ divides by the standard deviation (12), not the variance (144).

explanation: z = 1.00, so the upper-tail probability is 1 − 0.8413 = 15.87%, which matches the 16% one-sigma tail.

stem: Returns on a Banff tourism stock are roughly normal with a mean of 9.0% and a standard deviation of 12.0%. Using the cumulative normal table, what is the probability that the annual return falls between 0% and 24%, in %?

errors.label: Reported only N(1.25)
errors.explain: N(1.25) is P(R < 24%), which includes returns below 0%; subtract the lower tail.

errors.label: Subtracted N(0.75) instead of N(−0.75)
errors.explain: The lower bound is below the mean: N(−0.75) = 1 − N(0.75), not N(0.75).

explanation: P(between) = N(upper z) − N(lower z) = 0.8944 − 0.2266 = 66.78%.

stem: Annual returns on a fund are roughly normal with a mean of 7.5% and a standard deviation of 11.0%. Which range contains about 95% of annual returns?
explanation: 95% corresponds to two standard deviations: 7.5 ± 2 × 11.0 = 7.5 ± 22.0 = −14.5% to 29.5%. −3.5% to 18.5% is ±1σ (68%), −25.5% to 40.5% is ±3σ (99%), and −22.0% to 22.0% forgets to centre on the mean.

stem: Annual returns on a Canadian bond fund are roughly normal with a mean of 6.0% and a standard deviation of 12.0%. Using the cumulative normal table, what is the probability of a negative return in a year?
explanation: z = (0 − 6.0)/12.0 = −0.50 and N(−0.50) = 1 − N(0.50) = 1 − 0.6915 = 30.85%. Using N(0.50) directly gives 69.15%; dividing by the variance (z ≈ −0.04) gives 48.40%; 16% applies only at exactly one σ below the mean.
